Q_EC.text: The conversation actually went better than I expected -- I had been building up the courage for a few weeks before I finally brought it up with my manager, and when I did (I framed it as "I have anxiety and I want to be upfront about how it sometimes affects my work") she was genuinely receptive and didn't make it feel clinical or like a performance review. she asked what would actually help, which I thought was exactly the right question, and we ended up agreeing on a few concrete things: flexible start times on days when the anxiety is particularly rough, the option to work from home when I need a quieter environment, and a standing check-in every couple of weeks just to see how things are going. What really struck me was that she mentioned, sort of in passing, that she herself had gone through a period of burnout and understood why it mattered to address this stuff early rather than waiting until it becomes a crisis -- and that openness on her part made me feel like I wasn't just being accommodated as a logistical problem, I was being actually understood, which is honestly a different thing entirely. I've tried to be open about that experience with colleagues since then because I think knowing it can go well makes it easier for others to have the same conversation

Q_CC.text: It happened more gradually with coworkers than it did with my manager -- there wasn't one big conversation, it was more like a series of small moments where I let a bit more out each time and the response was positive enough that I kept going. The first time was with a colleague I sit near, I mentioned offhandedly that I was working from home that day because my anxiety had been bad, just sort of matter-of-fact about it, and instead of the awkward silence I half-expected she said something like "yeah, I've had weeks like that too" and we ended up talking for a while about how the open-plan office makes it worse (which it absolutely does, at least for me). After that it felt like the seal was broken in a good way, and a few other people on the team have since mentioned their own experiences to me -- one colleague has depression and hadn't told anyone at work before, and she told me that seeing me be open about it made her feel like it was okay to say something. that's honestly the part that matters most to me, because I think the stigma around this stuff survives on silence, and every small disclosure that goes well is kind of a crack in it

Q_CW.text: The one that stands out most is the colleague I mentioned -- she came to me one afternoon when the rest of the team had gone for lunch and it was just the two of us in the office, and she started by saying she'd been watching how I talked about my anxiety and wanted to ask how I'd decided to be so open about it, because she had been dealing with depression for couple of years and hadn't told anyone at work. She was quite tentative at first, choosing her words carefully, and I just tried to listen without jumping in too quickly because I think sometimes people need to get the whole thing out before they want a response. she said the thing she was most afraid of was being seen as unreliable professionally -- like she'd suddenly be handled differently, given easier work or left out of things -- and I recognized that fear immediately because I'd felt exactly the same before my own conversation with our manager. We ended up talking for probably an hour, and at some point she shifted from hesitant to almost relieved, like saying it out loud had taken some of the weight off. I don't know if she's talked to anyone else since, but I really hope she has

Q_PE.text:
My previous employer was a different story, and honestly I think that contrast is part of why I was so deliberate about having the conversation early at my current job -- I'd learned from the first attempt what it looks like when it doesn't go particularly well. I was at that company for about two years and I waited almost the whole time before saying anything, partly because the culture there was very "push through it" and I just didn't feel like there was space for that kind of disclosure, and when I finally did raise it (I'd had a rough few weeks and my work was starting to show it, so I felt like I had to say something) the reaction from my manager was polite but pretty surface-level. he said something along the lines of "thanks for letting me know, let me know if you need anything" and that was essentially it -- no follow-up, no check-in, nothing changed in any practical way. I don't think he was unkind, I think he just genuinely didn't know what to do with the information and defaulted to treating it as a box that had now been ticked. The HR person I spoke to separately was a bit more engaged but the only concrete thing that came out of it was a leaflet about the employee assistance programme, which I appreciated in principle but felt a bit like being handed a pamphlet when what you actually needed was a conversation. I left that job for other reasons but I won't pretend the experience didn't contribute to the feeling that it was time to find somewhere that handled these things differently -- and thankfully I did
</s>

Q_PC.text: At the previous job I was much more guarded, so there wasn't really an equivalent of the gradual opening-up I described with my current team -- I think because the overall culture was so "heads down, get on with it" that even casual personal conversation felt slightly out of place, let alone anything about mental health. I had one friend there, someone I'd started at the same time as, and I told her at some point during that rough patch near the end of my time there, mostly because I was visibly struggling and she'd asked directly if I was okay (and when someone asks you directly it's harder to deflect). Her reaction was genuinely warm -- she didn't make it weird, she just said she'd had no idea and asked what she could do, which was kind of her even if the honest answer was "not much, this isn't something you can fix." beyond her I didn't say anything to anyone else, partly because I hadn't figured out yet that being open was actually a reasonable option, and partly because I think I'd internalized the culture of that place more than I realized at the time. looking back, I wish I'd had more of those conversations earlier because the isolation of keeping it private definitely made everything feel heavier -- but I also think you need to feel like the environment is safe before you can take that risk, and at that job I just didn't have enough evidence that it was

Q_CA.text: The honest answer is that it hasn't affected my career negatively in any concrete way -- at least not at my current job, where being open about my anxiety has actually made things better in some measurable sense because the accommodations mean I'm more consistently productive than I was when I was just quietly struggling and pretending everything was fine. there was a period after the conversation at my previous employer where I did wonder if I'd made myself more visible in a bad way, like whether I'd be overlooked for things without being told that was the reason, but nothing happened that I could point to as clear evidence of that and eventually I stopped watching for it. What I think the experience has done -- and I mean this in a genuinely positive way -- is made me more deliberate about what kind of environments I'm willing to work in, which I'd argue is a career benefit even if it doesn't show up on a CV. Knowing what good looks like means I can recognise bad earlier and make choices accordingly, and I think that self-awareness has made me a better advocate for myself in general. The stigma-reduction part of it has if anything made me more connected to people on my teams, not less, because once you've had those conversations you have relationships with actual depth rather than just working relationships, and that kind of trust tends to help rather than hurt when it comes to collaboration and how people think of you professionally

Q_BH.text:
The one I'd point to is the conversation at my previous employer, specifically the sequence of things that happened -- or didn't happen -- after I finally said something. The circumstances were that I'd had a particularly difficult few weeks, my work was slipping in ways that were becoming visible, and I felt like I had to get ahead of it before my manager noticed and drew his own conclusions, so I asked for a brief one-to-one and explained that I'd been dealing with anxiety and that it had been harder to manage than usual lately. The conversation itself was probably fifteen minutes and he was polite throughout, which I want to be fair about, but the response was so thin that it almost felt worse than silence -- there was no curiosity, no follow-up questions, just "thanks for telling me, let me know if there's anything you need" and then we moved on to talking about a deadline. I waited a couple of weeks to see if anything would change and nothing did, no check-in, no acknowledgment that the conversation had even happened, so I went to HR separately hoping for something more substantive and got an employee assistance programme leaflet and a website address. I don't think anyone was actively trying to be dismissive, which is almost the frustrating part, because it means there was no one to be angry at -- it was just institutional indifference dressed up as a process, and the practical effect was that I felt more alone with it after the disclosure than I had before, which is sort of the worst possible outcome when you've finally worked up the nerve to say something
</s>

Q_SH.text: The circumstances I'd point to are really the conversation with my current manager, which I've described a bit already but which deserves more detail here because I think the specific things she did right are worth naming. I'd asked for a one-to-one by email and kept the subject line deliberately vague because I still wasn't sure how it was going to go, and when we sat down I had kind of a mental script prepared -- I wanted to explain what anxiety actually is for me in practical terms, not just say "I have anxiety" and leave her to fill in the blanks, so I talked about what a difficult morning looks like and how it affects my ability to concentrate in open-plan settings and why flexible start times would actually help rather than just being a perk. And she listened to all of it, like really listened, and then the first thing she said was "what would actually help you, practically?" which sounds simple but is honestly the right question because it treated me as the expert on my own condition rather than making assumptions about what accommodation should look like. the outcome was concrete -- flexible starts, work from home as needed, fortnightly check-ins -- and the follow-through has been consistent, she hasn't let those check-ins drop even when things are busy. But I think what made it feel genuinely well-handled rather than just procedurally correct was the moment she mentioned her own experience with burnout, because that small act of reciprocal openness changed the register of the whole conversation from "manager accommodating an employee" to "two people talking honestly about something real," and that distinction matters more than I can quite articulate

Q_ID.text:
The thing I keep coming back to is the difference between having a policy and actually having a culture, because I've worked somewhere that had both the EAP leaflet and the website address and it was the loneliest I've ever felt after a disclosure, and I've worked somewhere where none of that was particularly formalised but my manager happened to be a person who knew how to have a real conversation -- and the second experience was incomparably better. So I think the structural answer is that training matters, specifically training managers not in HR compliance but in how to actually respond when someone tells them something hard, how to ask good questions, how to follow up, how to not just tick the box and move on. The conversation I had at my current job went well largely because my manager was good at listening, and I don't think that was an accident -- I think she'd thought about it.

Beyond that I do think normalisation at the industry level is the lever that moves everything else, because the stigma around mental health in tech in particular is still real even if it's less visible than it used to be, and the most powerful thing that changes stigma is hearing that other people have been through the same thing and that it went okay. So senior people being willing to say something publicly, or companies creating actual space for those conversations rather than just a wellness app subscription, would matter. and honestly flexible working arrangements as a genuine default rather than an accommodation you have to negotiate for individually would remove so much of the burden from people who are already managing something hard
</s>

Q_AE.text: I suppose the thing I'd most want to add is that I filled this out because I think research like this actually matters -- not in a vague "raising awareness" way but in the specific sense that having data about what people actually experience is the only way to move the conversation past anecdote. I've been lucky enough to have a genuinely good experience, and I'm aware that's not the norm, and I think the gap between what's possible (a manager who asks the right question, a team where disclosure is normal) and what most people actually get is the thing worth closing. so I hope whoever reads these responses finds something useful in them, and if my particular experience of it going well is a data point that's helpful, then that's the best possible use of the hour I've spent thinking through all of this. also -- and this is maybe a minor thing -- I'd gently suggest that future versions of this survey include a question about what specifically made a response feel supportive versus just procedurally correct, because I think that distinction is where the most useful information lives and it's a bit hard to convey in the current structure

Q_EC.text: Was having a particularly bad anxiety episode that had lasted a few days and was negatively affecting work so I asked if I could take a few days off, and explained why. He said yes, and we now have open communication about my illness and he allows me some "exceptions" from rules. Such as I have more flexible work hours, and I can work from home when I need to. I can take "anxiety days" when I need to. I do take them unpaid since that gives me less anxiety and then it doesn't show on the budget higher up (A large company has a small office in my country and these are all arrangements at that office.) but he is fine with me taking them as paid sick days, again my choice not to do so. All I have to do is inform my team when I'm showing up very late or not at all or working from home, it is such a relief to be able to have honest open communication and has lessened a lot of anxiety that I had about "being sick a lot" or if they thought I was a lazy person. My anxiety also affects my sleep a lot and now since making these adjustments I have not had to show up for work unslept and the even though I have fewer hours some weeks then I did before they are more productive and I'm happier about them. He did ask a lot about if there was anything at work that was making things worse and what they could do better, and when they were changing up teams at my office I was asked before anything was finalized.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager I was seeing a therapist and asked if the company's EAP covered ongoing sessions. He was actually pretty receptive -- no awkwardness, just asked what I needed. Q_CW.text: The same coworker I mentioned eventually opened up more directly -- said they'd been dealing with anxiety for a while but had never told anyone at work. They weren't in crisis or anything, just carrying it quietly. I tried to make it easy by sharing that therapy had been straightforward for me to access, though I know cost is prohibitive for some people without good coverage.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job the culture was pretty different -- I mentioned I was in therapy during a check-in and my manager sort of nodded and moved on, no follow-up, no offer of resources. Q_PC.text: At my previous job I didn't really bring it up with coworkers the way I do now -- the environment just didn't feel like it invited that kind of openness. I mentioned once to a teammate that I had a therapy appointment and they kind of just said "oh cool" and changed the subject. Not unkind, but definitely not a place where that conversation was gonna go anywhere.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, not negatively -- at least not that I'm aware of. I've been deliberate about how I bring it up, which probably helps. If anything, being open about therapy has made me someone colleagues feel comfortable coming to, which feels like a net positive. I'm sure there are workplaces where it would've played out differently, but I've been lucky in that regard

Q_BH.text: Probably the previous manager situation -- I mentioned therapy during a check-in and got a polite nod and that was it. No resources offered, no follow-up, just moved on. I don't think it was intentional, but polite indifference still signals pretty clearly that the topic isn't really welcome, and that's honestly enough to keep someone quiet going forward

Q_SH.text: The conversation with my current manager stands out. I came in with a specific ask — whether the EAP would cover more than the standard sessions -- and instead of deflecting or making it weird, he just engaged with it directly. Asked what I needed, followed up with HR, and within a week there was actually a resolution. it felt like talking to someone who understood that mental health support is just... a normal thing to accommodate, not a sensitive situation to be carefully managed around.

Q_ID.text: The biggest lever is probably making coverage genuinely adequate — not just an EAP that covers three sessions and calls it done. Subsidized or sliding-scale therapy options, real parity in insurance coverage. Beyond cost, I think normalizing the conversation matters as much as the benefits themselves: managers who know how to respond when someone brings it up without making it weird or just nodding and moving on. that cultural piece is harder to mandate but honestly just as important

Q_AE.text: I just want to say that surveys like this matter -- the fact that someone is trying to measure this stuff systematically feels like part of the same work. Stigma doesn't go away on its own; it goes away when people talk, when employers respond well, when cost isn't the thing that stops someone from getting help. Appreciate the chance to weigh in.

Q_SH.text: The accommodation conversation with my direct manager at that same job, once I finally had it. I explained what actually helps -- fewer context switches, longer focus blocks -- and they just made it happen. No bureaucracy, no drama. they adjusted the sprint board and that was that.

Q_ID.text: Normalize it the way you'd normalize any other health issue. Clear accommodation processes, managers trained to actually handle disclosures instead of escalating out of panic, and -- honestly -- just not making it weird when someone brings it up.

Q_EC.text: The most substantive conversation was with HR, after a situation at work had been escalating for months. I told them I was experiencing PTSD symptoms -- being that direct was uncomfortable, honestly, but it felt necessary to get the right support. They arranged some adjustments to my environment and referred me to the EAP. Q_CW.text: One colleague came to me after my talk on anxiety -- I think hearing someone speak openly made it feel safer for them to do the same. They described feeling overwhelmed and burned out, and were worried that saying anything to management would affect how they were perceived. I mostly just listened and shared what I'd found helpful in terms of practical steps, like talking to the EAP. I don't know exactly what they did after that conversation, but they seemed a bit less alone in it, which I hope counted for something.

Q_PE.text: With my previous employer, the conversation was harder and less productive. I tried to raise concerns about my working environment -- which was, at that point, genuinely unsafe -- and the response was largely dismissive. There was no referral, no adjustment, just a suggestion that I try to manage better. That experience is part of why I was more deliberate about how I approached things at my next job.

Q_PC.text: At the previous job, I was a lot more guarded -- the environment didn't feel safe enough for that kind of openness. Q_CA.text: It's been mixed, honestly. Being open about anxiety has created some unexpected professional connections -- the talk led to conversations I found genuinely useful, and I think being visible on the topic has made certain colleagues more comfortable coming to me. Q_BH.text: The situation at my previous job involved a colleague whose behavior had escalated to the point where I genuinely feared for my physical safety. When I raised this with management, the response was essentially that I was probably misreading things, and I should try to address it directly with the person involved. No investigation, no interim measures -- nothing that acknowledged what I was actually describing. The suggestion to "manage better" when I was already struggling to feel safe came across as a kind of institutional shrug, and honestly it delayed me getting any real support by several months.

Q_SH.text: When I spoke to HR at my current job about the PTSD, they listened without minimizing what I was describing -- which was, honestly, already a meaningful contrast. They followed up with concrete steps: environmental adjustments and a referral to the EAP. My manager was looped in with appropriate discretion. It didn't fix everything overnight, but I felt like the institution was actually responding rather than just waiting for the problem to go away.

Q_ID.text: The biggest gap I've seen is between stated policy and actual practice. Most organizations have an EAP listed somewhere, but whether a manager knows how to respond when someone actually discloses -- that's a different question entirely. More consistent training for managers, not just HR, would help. And honestly, the industry's culture around productivity and resilience still makes it harder than it should be to say "I'm not okay" without worrying it'll be held against you. the structural piece matters too: accessible, confidential support that doesn't require a crisis to trigger.

Q_AE.text: One thing that wasn't quite captured here is how much informal peer support mattered alongside the formal structures -- colleagues who just knew and checked in without making it a thing. The EAP referral helped, but honestly the day-to-day stability came more from that. I'd also add that recovery while continuing to work is nonlinear; weeks that felt like progress could still be disrupted by an unexpected interaction or meeting. workplaces that can accommodate that variability, not just the initial crisis, are rare but make a real difference.

Q_EC.text: I had a conversation with my direct supervisor during a particularly difficult period. Their response was measured -- they acknowledged what I shared but stopped short of any formal accommodation or follow-up. Honestly, the expectation seemed to be that I'd just manage it privately. I dont think anyone acted in bad faith, but the support was more symbolic than substantive

Q_CC.text: Most of the conversations I've had with coworkers went in the other direction -- they came to me rather than the other way around. I've had direct reports and a few peers share some fairly serious struggles, substance-related issues included, and I tried to respond thoughtfully. When it comes to my own situation, I've kept that pretty close. Partly instinct, partly an awareness of how these things tend to move around an organization once they're out there.

Q_CW.text: One conversation that stayed with me involved a direct report who came to me after hours, clearly having held this in for a while. They disclosed that they were navigating a dependency issue and had started outpatient treatment -- they weren't asking for anything formal, just needed someone to know. I tried to respond in a way that acknowledged the trust without making it transactional. I let them lead on what, if anything, they wanted documented or escalated, and mostly just listened. It stayed between us.

Q_PE.text: At a previous company, earlier in my career, I did raise something -- not framed explicitly as a mental health concern, but that's what it was. The response was fairly perfunctory: HR pointed me to an EAP, my manager suggested taking a few days off. Nothing was followed up on after that. I think that experience shaped how selective I became about what I share and with whom, honestly more than I'd like to admit.

Q_PC.text: At that company, I didn't bring much to coworkers directly. There was one colleague I was close with who could tell something was off, and they checked in a few times -- genuinely, not just in passing. I appreciated that. But I kept the details vague, mostly because I wasn't sure how far it would travel. kinda learned from watching others that those conversations don't always stay where you leave them.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, I've been careful enough that I'm not sure I've been fully "identified" in any formal sense -- which is probably a calculated choice on my part. That said, I think there's a version of being known that happens informally, and I'm aware that some people have put pieces together. Whether that's affected opportunities or how I'm perceived, I genuinely can't say with certainty. What I do know is that the possibility of it has shaped how I present myself, probably more than it should.

Q_BH.text: The situation I'd point to was at my previous company. I raised something carefully -- not labeled explicitly as a mental health concern, but that's essentially what it was -- and the response was a referral to the EAP and a suggestion to take a few days. What stayed with me wasn't the advice itself, which was generic but not harmful. It was the complete absence of any follow-through. Nobody checked back in a week later, no one acknowledged it again. The conversation simply closed, and the implicit message was that the matter had been handled. that kind of closure-by-default communicates something pretty clearly about how much the organization actually wants to engage with it.

Q_SH.text: The clearest example I can point to is actually the colleague I mentioned -- the one who noticed something was off and checked in without making it a production. What made it work was the absence of any agenda. They weren't trying to fix anything or document anything. They just made space. honestly that's rarer than it should be, and it's shaped how I try to show up when someone comes to me.

Q_ID.text: The most meaningful change would be building in actual follow-through -- not just having resources available, but having someone check back in after a disclosure. The EAP referral as an endpoint has to stop being the default. Beyond that, I think managers need real training on how to hold these conversations without immediately routing them to HR. Not because HR shouldn't be involved, but because the instinct to escalate or document can shut things down before they've even started. Creating space for informal support, without it automatically becoming a process, would go a long way.

Q_AE.text: One thing I'd add is that the dual position of being someone who has navigated mental health challenges personally while also being someone others come to with their own creates a particular kind of complexity that doesn't get discussed much. The informal support role that a lot of managers quietly fill -- without training, without structure, and often without anyone checking in on them -- is a real gap. it's a lot to carry, and I'm not sure the industry has fully reckoned with what it's asking of people in that position.

Q_EC.text: i told my manager i was struggling with depression and was in early recovery thinking it would at least explain some of what i was going through. he seemed supportive in the moment, said all the right things about flexibility. then it showed up in my performance review -- framed as concerns about reliability and commitment. that was a gut punch. i learned pretty fast that openness with management doesn't always protect you

Q_CC.text: coworkers were a completely different story, honestly. a few of them had gone through their own stuff and were upfront about it, which made it easier to open up. one guy i worked closely with had dealt with depression too and we just kind of... started checking in on each other. it felt like actual solidarity rather than HR-speak. those friendships got me through some of the harder stretches in a way that management never could

Q_CW.text: he came to me first, actually. we'd been working late together on a rough sprint and he just kind of let it out -- said he'd been on medication for a while and was worried about what would happen if anyone at work found out. i think he trusted me because i'd already hinted at my own stuff. it meant a lot that he felt safe enough to say it.

Q_PE.text: the previous job was actually less dramatic about it. i didn't disclose much -- just mentioned i was dealing with some health stuff and needed to adjust my schedule temporarily. they were pretty hands-off, which i think i preferred at the time. no real conversation happened, just a nod and a schedule change. looking back i'm not sure if that was respect for my privacy or just indifference

Q_PC.text: at that job i kept it pretty close to the chest, so there wasn't much of a conversation to speak of. a couple of coworkers knew something was off -- you can't hide everything -- and one of them checked in once, asked if i was okay. i said yeah, mostly fine. she didn't push and i didn't offer more. it was kind, just... surface level

Q_CA.text: it set me back at that job, honestly. whatever goodwill i'd built with management evaporated pretty fast once i put a name to what i was going through -- the performance review made that clear enough. i dont know if it cost me a specific promotion but it definitely changed how i was perceived. i'm more careful now about who i tell, even though i havent gone fully silent about it

Q_BH.text: it was the performance review, about three months after i'd opened up to my manager. he'd been so measured and reasonable in the moment -- said he appreciated me being honest, that we'd figure it out together. then i'm sitting across from him reading comments about "inconsistent follow-through" and "questions about long-term commitment to the role." nothing was said directly, but i knew exactly what it referred to. he never even brought it up to my face.

Q_SH.text: the coworker i mentioned -- the one we'd been doing late sprints with -- handled it better than anyone. when i eventually told him more about the depression and the recovery piece, he didn't flinch or get weird about it. just said "yeah, that makes sense, i'm glad you're still here." that was it. no advice, no pivoting to solutions. just acknowledgment. honestly that meant more to me than any formal accommodation ever did

Q_EC.text: I told my manager directly that I'd been having panic attacks during crunch periods. he was receptive -- suggested I block recovery time into my calendar and connected me with the EAP. Honestly it went better than I expected.

Q_BH.text: At my previous employer, I flagged burnout pretty explicitly -- panic attacks, disrupted sleep, the works. My manager nodded, said it sounded rough, and that was essentially it. No follow-up, no workload adjustment. it just got dropped like it never came up.

Q_SH.text: The turnaround came at my current job. When I told my manager about the panic attacks, he actually followed up the next day -- checked in, adjusted my sprint load, and made sure I knew the EAP was a real option, not just fine print. It felt like being actually heard.

Q_AE.text: I think the survey covers the key dimensions well. One thing I'd add is that peer-led mental health advocates -- not just formal EAPs -- can make a real difference. Sometimes people will talk to a trusted colleague long before they'd ever call a helpline.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager I had anxiety, pretty matter-of-factly about it. She nodded, said she'd keep it in mind. I suppose that counted as a reaction. the team was falling apart anyway so it kind of got lost in all that -- no real follow-up came of it.

Q_CC.text: Mentioned it to a couple of colleagues, same way I did with my manager -- just kind of said I have anxiety, not a big deal. they were pretty normal about it, one guy said he had it too. the dysfunction in the office honestly overshadowed any of that pretty quickly.

Q_CW.text: One of my teammates mentioned they were dealing with depression, pretty offhand, like we were talking about the chaos in the office anyway and it just came up. I said that makes sense given the environment honestly. it wasn't a deep conversation, more just acknowledging reality.

Q_PE.text: Similar story really, maybe even less eventful. Brought it up once, the manager at the time kind of just nodded and moved on. I suppose I wasn't expecting much. it's just not something companies actually deal with, they acknowledge it and then nothing changes.

Q_PC.text: Pretty much the same as the current job honestly. Mentioned the anxiety to a few people, no one made it weird. one guy said something like "yeah makes sense in this industry" and that was kind of it. there was enough actual dysfunction to distract from anything personal going on.

Q_CA.text: Honestly it hasn't been a huge deal, I think because I've always framed it pretty casually. no one's treated me differently in any obvious way. the bigger career hits have come from just working in chaotic places -- that kind of thing follows you more than an anxiety disclosure does.

Q_BH.text: I suppose the worst part wasn't hostility, it was just nothing. Told my manager, she acknowledged it, and then that was genuinely the end of it. no check-in, no accommodation offered, just absorbed into the general chaos. kind of hard to call it badly handled when there was no handling at all.

Q_SH.text: Honestly the best response I got was from a colleague, not management. when I mentioned the anxiety he just said "yeah me too, it's a lot" and we kind of moved on. I suppose that was it -- no big moment, but it felt real. sometimes that's enough.

Q_ID.text: Actually do something after you acknowledge it, I suppose that's the main thing. every company has the policy, the EAP number, whatever -- but no one follows up. a manager who checks in once would do more than any wellness program. it's not complicated, it's just that no one bothers.

Q_AE.text: I guess what doesn't quite get captured is how much general dysfunction amplifies all of it. it's hard to separate mental health stuff from just bad management, they feed each other. honestly the mental health piece can feel almost secondary when the whole environment is on fire around you.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager I was dealing with PTSD and needed some flexibility with my schedule. they adjusted my hours and kept it off the record.

Q_CC.text: Mentioned it to a couple of close coworkers. they were fine with it, asked if there was anything they could do.

Q_CW.text: One coworker told me they were struggling with anxiety and burnout. I just listened, didn't make it weird. suggested they talk to HR about accommodations.

Q_PE.text: Similar situation. Disclosed burnout and some trauma history, they were receptive. Moved me off a high-pressure project for a few months.

Q_PC.text: Brought it up briefly with a few people on the old team. they didn't make a big deal of it, just kind of acknowledged it and moved on.

Q_CA.text: It hasn't, as far as I can tell. Both employers handled it professionally and nothing changed in terms of responsibilities or advancement.

Q_SH.text: Both times I disclosed, management kept it private and made reasonable adjustments without treating it as a performance issue.

Q_ID.text: Clearer policies on disclosure and accommodation would help. most people dont know what they're entitled to, and that gap causes unnecessary stress.

Q_AE.text: Trauma disclosure in professional settings is still under-supported by most HR frameworks. That's the main gap I see.
